questions.stem: Which device converts the sound wave into the electrical signal shown on the oscilloscope?

options.explanation: The microphone detects the sound and turns it into an electrical signal.
The screen displays the signal; it does not capture it.
A tuning fork makes sound; it does not detect it.
The time base sets the horizontal scale; it detects nothing.

questions.stem: What does the horizontal axis (time base) of the oscilloscope allow you to measure?

options.explanation: Amplitude is read vertically, from the centre line.

options.text: the time period of the wave
options.explanation: The horizontal axis is time, so one full cycle spans the time period.
Loudness is linked to amplitude, which is vertical.
Nothing on the screen identifies material.

questions.stem: A second sound is played with a higher frequency than the first. What changes on the screen if the time base is unchanged?

options.explanation: Frequency is exactly what the horizontal axis displays.
Frequency is a horizontal, cycle-count property.

options.text: more complete waves fit on the screen
options.explanation: Higher frequency packs more cycles into the same time window.

options.text: fewer complete waves fit on the screen
options.explanation: That is what a LOWER frequency does.

questions.stem: A trace rises and falls gently with a large height from the centre line. What does that indicate about the sound?

options.text: ultrasound, because the wave is tall
options.explanation: Nothing on screen alone names the frequency band.
Height indicates amplitude (loudness), not pitch.
The gentle rise and fall suggests a long period, but the large height means loud; the pitch claim does not follow from height alone.

options.text: large amplitude, so a loud sound
options.explanation: Height measured from the centre is the amplitude, and amplitude carries loudness.

questions.stem: Besides a sound wave, which signal is named as something an oscilloscope can display?

options.explanation: Alternating current is the second named rapidly changing signal.
Friction is not a signal at all.
Field lines are diagrams, not time signals.

options.text: a steady direct current from a battery
options.explanation: A steady d.c. is not a rapidly changing signal.

questions.stem: State what a microphone does in this set-up.
questions.modelAnswer: It detects the sound wave and converts it into an electrical signal that the oscilloscope can display.

questions.stem: State what the trace height, taken from the screen’s centre line, is related to.
questions.modelAnswer: The trace height shows the amplitude of the sound wave.

questions.stem: Explain why a sound wave, which is longitudinal in air, can be displayed as a transverse-looking trace on an oscilloscope.
questions.modelAnswer: The oscilloscope does not draw the air itself; it plots the microphone’s electrical signal against time. Pressure variations of the longitudinal wave become voltage ups and downs along the time axis, so the displayed trace has the peak-and-trough shape of a transverse wave even though the air vibrations are along the direction of travel.

questions.stem: Two traces are frozen on the same screen. Trace X shows six complete cycles and trace Y shows two complete cycles in the same width. Compare the pitch of the two sounds.
questions.modelAnswer: Trace X shows more cycles in the same time, so it has the higher frequency, and since pitch rises with frequency, X is the higher-pitched sound while Y is the lower-pitched one.
